主要内容: The article discusses a growing conflict over ownership of real estate affected by climate change, particularly in areas prone to flooding. In Dauphin Island, Alabama, and Louisiana, rising sea levels and coastal erosion are submerging land, creating new waterways and altering property boundaries. Daryl Carpenter, a charter boat captain from Grand Isle, Louisiana, encountered a dispute when another boat owner claimed he was trespassing on a newly formed pond. The sheriff’s office threatened to arrest Carpenter for returning to the area, despite Louisiana state law stating that any waterways accessible by boat are considered public property. This case highlights the legal and ownership challenges arising from climate change impacts on coastal real estate.
